title: Foundations
intro: The language of quantum mechanics, taught from the ground up, and its first rules: states are unit vectors of complex amplitudes, measurements give random results with probabilities from the Born rule, and measurable quantities are Hermitian operators. Eight pages, from the experiments that started it to the uncertainty relation.

blocks.text: Quantum mechanics is a set of rules for predicting the results of experiments on small systems: atoms, photons, electrons, and the qubits of a quantum computer or a quantum reservoir. The rules are short, but they are written in a language most people have not met: complex numbers, vectors and matrices. This chapter teaches that language from the ground up and then uses it to state the first rules: what a state is, what happens when you measure it, and what an observable quantity is.

Nothing here depends on a particular physical system. The examples are mostly qubits, the simplest quantum systems, because a qubit's state is just two complex numbers and every calculation can be done by hand. The next chapter, Qubits (#/quantum/qubits), then studies the qubit itself in depth.

Read the pages in order; each assumes the ones before it. Each page starts with what you need first and what you will be able to do, has a short 'Check yourself' question at the end of every main section, and closes with problems that have full solutions. Do the check questions before reading on: they are short, and the later sections build on them. Expect each page to take an hour or two with pencil and paper. If you already know complex numbers and linear algebra, read the experiments page, skim pages two to four (complex numbers, linear algebra, eigenvalues) for the notation, and start in earnest at States and Dirac Notation.

items: Why Quantum Mechanics: The Experiments (#/quantum/foundations/why-quantum): the experiments that classical physics cannot explain, Stern-Gerlach magnets, polarising filters and single particles that interfere with themselves, and the ideas (amplitudes, superposition, probabilistic outcomes) they force on us.

Complex Numbers for Quantum Mechanics (#/quantum/foundations/complex-numbers): adding, multiplying and conjugating complex numbers, the polar form $re^{i\theta}$, and why quantum amplitudes need the phase $\theta$.

Linear Algebra for Quantum Mechanics (#/quantum/foundations/linear-algebra): vectors with complex entries, inner products and lengths, matrices as transformations, Hermitian and unitary matrices, and the tensor product that joins two systems.

Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (#/quantum/foundations/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors): the directions a matrix only stretches, how to find them for $2\times2$ matrices by hand, the spectral theorem, and functions of a matrix such as $e^{-iHt}$.

States and Dirac Notation (#/quantum/foundations/states-and-dirac-notation): kets $\vert\psi\rangle$ and bras $\langle\psi\vert$, superposition, changing basis, and why an overall phase does not matter while a relative phase does.

Measurement and the Born Rule (#/quantum/foundations/measurement): how amplitudes turn into probabilities, what a measurement does to the state, measuring in other bases, and how many repetitions (shots) an estimate needs.

Observables and Uncertainty (#/quantum/foundations/observables-and-uncertainty): measurable quantities as Hermitian operators, the average result $\langle A\rangle$ and the spread $\sigma_A$, and the uncertainty relation for two quantities.

Commutators and Compatible Observables (#/quantum/foundations/commutators): the commutator $[A, B]$, which observables can be measured together, the derivation of the uncertainty relation, $[x, p] = i$, and conserved quantities.

blocks.text: These are the equations the chapter builds up to. Each line says what it means; the pages above say why.

blocks.caption: A state is a unit vector: complex amplitudes c_k on a basis, with squared sizes adding to 1.
The inner product: how much of one state lies along another. Its squared size is a probability.
An eigenvector of A is only stretched, by its eigenvalue λ. Measurement results are eigenvalues.
The Born rule: the probability of outcome k when measuring in the basis {|e_k⟩}.
The average result of measuring A, and the spread of the results.
The uncertainty relation: quantities whose operators do not commute cannot both be sharp.

blocks.text: The postulates still missing after this chapter are how states change in time (the Schrödinger equation, in Dynamics (#/quantum/dynamics)) and how to describe several systems at once (Many Qubits (#/quantum/many-body)). In between, Qubits (#/quantum/qubits) turns the general rules into a picture you can see, the Bloch sphere, and into the gates of a quantum computer.

If you are heading for the QRC shelf and only have time for one page here, read Measurement and the Born Rule. The fact that a feature like $\langle Z\rangle$ must be estimated from many destructive shots shapes half of what quantum reservoir hardware can and cannot do.
